content: The process of evaluating the magnitude of both desirable and undesirable effects of a specific intervention involves a detailed analysis that extends beyond the certainty of the evidence assessed. It also considers how individuals directly affected by the intervention value its outcomes, including its implications for resources, cost-effectiveness, equity, feasibility, and acceptability. For this update, the desirable and undesirable effects of the interventions were assessed using previously described analytical methods. Additional critical factors that could guide the judgments of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) in making evidence-informed assessments were also taken into account. Evidence reviews on cost-effectiveness, values, preferences, and acceptability were commissioned to support the decision-making process and the conclusions drawn regarding the interventions under evaluation, such as electrocardiography and audiometry. A decision-analytic model was employed to provide insights into the implementation of these recommendations. This model assessed the cost implications of changes to recommended regimens for drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB), estimated cost-effectiveness, and identified parameters and characteristics that could influence cost or cost-effectiveness. The focus was on the use of an all-oral, bedaquiline-containing shorter regimen of 9–12 months and the extended use of bedaquiline beyond six months in combination with delamanid. Transmission models for secondary cases prevented by more effective treatment and Markov cost-effectiveness models for the total costs of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) cases were also utilized. Costs were evaluated from a health system perspective. An economic evaluation was conducted to estimate the cost-effectiveness of a new regimen containing bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL) compared to the standard of care for patients with extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) or those who failed or were intolerant to MDR-TB treatments. This evaluation was performed in three epidemiological settings at a given price. A Markov model was developed to follow a cohort of the intended population for the BPaL regimen, allowing for the modeling of both disease and treatment processes, where the timing of events was critical. Clinical data from the Nix-TB study informed the clinical efficacy of the intervention, while costing estimates were derived from the Global Health Costing Consortium database and the Value-TB study. A qualitative study was conducted to better understand the values and preferences for treatment, as well as perspectives on treatment acceptability, feasibility, and equity. Although the goal was to gather evidence representing all individuals affected by the recommendations, including policymakers, health professionals, patients, and other stakeholders, the study primarily captured data from patient representatives and MDR/RR-TB survivors. The methodology involved in-depth interviews with stakeholders from high TB burden countries in Asia, Africa, Eastern Europe, and South America. Thematic findings reflecting values, preferences, and perspectives on the acceptability, feasibility, and equity of drug-resistant TB treatment are summarized in Figure A1. A separate evaluation of the BPaL regimen for treating XDR-TB patients or those intolerant to MDR-TB treatments was commissioned by the manufacturer and presented to the GDG. The quality of evidence was assessed using specific criteria, such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other considerations. Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is typically rated as high quality, while observational studies and programmatic data are often rated as low or very low quality. The higher the quality of evidence, the more likely a strong recommendation can be made. The strength of a recommendation is classified as either strong or conditional based on the balance between desirable and undesirable effects, values and preferences, resource use, equity considerations, acceptability, and feasibility. Strong recommendations indicate confidence that the desirable effects outweigh the undesirable effects, while conditional recommendations suggest that the desirable effects probably outweigh the undesirable effects. The WHO guideline development process incorporates quality assurance procedures, including assessments by the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre and a GRADE methodologist. Individual patient data (IPD)-based analyses were used to reduce between-study heterogeneity, examine patient-level characteristics, harmonize outcomes, and explore variability in effectiveness. However, residual confounding could still arise from unknown factors associated with both exposure and outcome for which data were not collected. The WHO guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) will be made freely available online and widely disseminated at international and regional conferences, as well as meetings of program managers. An operational guide with practical details will be released to support the programmatic implementation of the revised recommendations. National programs will be supported by WHO and technical and funding partners to prepare a national plan for managing drug-resistant TB. Implementers should create a conducive policy and programmatic environment, including national and local policies and standard operating procedures, to facilitate the implementation of these recommendations. This includes promoting universal health coverage and public financing for drug-resistant TB management, allocating dedicated resources, and training frontline healthcare staff in critical areas such as diagnosis, regimen design, patient support, treatment monitoring, and adverse reaction management. Meaningful engagement with affected populations, their communities, the private sector, and other relevant health programs and ministries is essential in planning and implementing the recommendations. The uptake of these WHO recommendations will be monitored through annual data collection by WHO Global TB Data Monitoring. The guidelines will be updated five years after publication or earlier if new evidence necessitates a revision.
